blocks.text: 1. Multi-Query Retrieval
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447443683-514871937.png
Query Transformation named the umbrella category. Multi-Query Retrieval applies query transformation at scale, searching with multiple query variations rather than committing to one rewrite.
It generates several differently phrased versions of the same question and searches with all of them.
2. One Question, Many Phrasings
A single question can be asked in many equally valid ways.
Multi-query retrieval searches with several of those phrasings at once instead of committing to just one.
3. Generating Query Variations
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447443683-987676855.png
As with expanding with an LLM in Query Expansion, a language model generates several distinct rephrasings of the original query.
Each variation emphasizes slightly different words or framing.
4. Searching Each Variation Separately
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447443684-994926036.png
Each query variation runs its own independent retrieval search.
This produces several separate ranked lists of candidate chunks.
5. Merging Results Across Variations
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447443684-224356440.png
As with reciprocal rank fusion in Hybrid Search, results from different query variations get merged using the same fusion techniques.
A chunk found by multiple phrasings rises higher in the combined ranking.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A chunk retrieved by three out of four query variations signals stronger relevance than a chunk found by only one phrasing, and reciprocal rank fusion reflects that agreement directly in the final ranking.

{"headers":["Chunk agreement across variations","Effect on merged ranking"],"rows":[["Found by one variation only","Ranks lower in the merged results"],["Found by multiple variations","Ranks higher, reflecting stronger agreement"]]}

blocks.text: 6. Covering Blind Spots Of A Single Phrasing
Any single phrasing of a query can miss a relevant chunk written with different terminology.
Multiple phrasings together cover far more of the retrieval space than one alone.
7. Multiplied Retrieval Cost
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447443685-313286375.png
As with the linear scaling problem in Brute Force Search, running N query variations means N separate retrieval searches.
That cost multiplies directly with how many variations get generated.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Generating five query variations and searching each one costs roughly five times the retrieval work of a single search, a real expense that has to be weighed against the improved coverage gained.

blocks.text: 8. Diminishing Returns With More Variations
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447443685-401822097.png
The first few extra variations catch the most additional relevant chunks.
Each additional variation beyond that adds cost with less and less additional benefit.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When Multi-Query Retrieval Is Worth The Added Cost

blocks.alt: Recognizing When Multi-Query Retrieval Is Worth The Added Cost
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447443685-946923347.png
High stakes queries where missing relevant content is costly justify multi-query retrieval.
Simple, low latency requirements may not justify running multiple searches per query.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Generating far more query variations than necessary, multiplying retrieval cost with little added benefit.
Never merging results across variations, treating each search as entirely separate.
Applying multi-query retrieval to every query regardless of latency requirements.
Generating query variations that are too similar to each other to add real coverage.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Multi-query retrieval generates several differently phrased versions of a question and searches with all of them.
A single question can be asked in many equally valid ways, and committing to one risks missing relevant chunks.
A language model generates several distinct rephrasings, each emphasizing different words or framing.
Each query variation runs its own independent retrieval search, producing separate ranked lists.
Results from different variations get merged using fusion techniques like reciprocal rank fusion.
A chunk found by multiple phrasings signals stronger relevance and rises higher in merged results.
Running N variations means N separate searches, multiplying retrieval cost directly.
The first few extra variations catch the most additional relevant chunks, with diminishing returns after.
